label: Expansion du nucléaire comme énergie de base décarbonée : doublement des capacités d'ici 2050

sources: IPCC AR6 SYR Figure 4.4 — Nuclear expansion mitigation potential ~1–1.5 GtCO2/yr in 2030 in electricity sector
IEA Nuclear Power and Secure Energy Transitions 2022 — Existing nuclear is the largest single source of low-carbon electricity; life extension is lowest-cost clean energy
IAEA Nuclear Energy for a Net Zero World — Net-zero 2050 requires doubling or tripling installed nuclear capacity
IPCC AR6 WGIII Ch.6 — Nuclear lifecycle emissions ~12 gCO2eq/kWh, comparable to wind, among lowest of all sources

planetary_limits.note: Nuclear waste remains hazardous for hundreds of thousands of years; no permanent repository operational globally except Finland

societal_indicators.note: Baseload nuclear provides grid stability complementary to variable renewables
Public opposition in many OECD countries constrains deployment; Fukushima legacy remains

interactions.note: Nuclear provides firm low-carbon baseload; renewables provide bulk capacity — complementary roles
Nuclear life extension accelerates coal closure by maintaining grid reliability during transition

methodological_note: Median impact of 1.5 GtCO2/yr calibrated against IPCC AR6 SYR Fig 4.4 nuclear electricity sector potential (~1–1.5 GtCO2/yr by 2030). Very long implementation lag (10 years) reflects typical 10–15 year construction timeline for large reactors; SMRs (Small Modular Reactors) could accelerate this. High uncertainty (score 3) reflects public opposition, cost overruns (Flamanville +€12bn, Hinkley Point C), and geopolitical constraints on nuclear proliferation. Energy mix deltas show nuclear gaining +4.5 pp share, displacing coal (-3.0 pp) and gas (-1.5 pp). Projection baseline: SSP2-4.5.
